items.title: Target booked $301 million from tariff refunds this quarter, nearly a fifth of its operating profit
items.summary:
After years of declining sales and dwindling store traffic , Target’s turnaround plan under CEO Michael Fiddelke is showing gains. The retail giant reported $26.45 billion in Q3 merchandise sales for the three months ending Oct. 31, up 6.9% from last year and beating analysts’ expectations of $25.96 billion. Operating profit was $1.67 billion, up 76% from last year and beating analysts’ expectations of $1.3 billion. 

But there’s a wrinkle: $301 million of that profit came from refunds of President Donald Trump’s tariffs, about 18% of the total, according to Target’s Q3 filing released on Nov. 18. Over the first nine months of this year, Target recognized $1.3 billion in tariff refunds following the Supreme Court’s ruling in February that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give the president authority to impose tariffs. 

Still, even without that windfall, Target seems to be recovering. Excluding the $301 million, Target would have reported about $1.37 billion in operating profit, still higher than the $948 million it recorded a year earlier. Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData Retail, told Fortune it’s a sign Target is genuinely gaining with consumers. 

“Tariff refunds are certainly very helpful to Target, and they have provided a very nice boost to the bottom line,” Saunders said. “That said, even if you take the tariff gain out, Target is still up on the prior year, and I think that really reflects the fact that the business does have some momentum on the consumer side.” 

He said Target’s investments in revamped stores and new products…
items.t: Target booked $301 million from tariff refunds this quarter, nearly a fifth of its operating profit

items.title: Want to build an AI operating model? First, build consensus
items.summary:
At a recent dinner with chief operating officers in New York City, we caught up with the senior leaders most often tasked with transforming AI use into value. The conversation was markedly different from the ones we were having just one year ago.

In 2025, peers in the C-suite would boast about individual AI successes: An agent that made software engineers more productive, or an AI use case in accounting that dethroned the spreadsheet.

But this year, conversations were focused on the forest, not the trees. Individual successes felt insufficient. The bigger question was: How do you do this again and again? How do you build a foundation that makes AI success second nature ?

Leaders want an AI Operating Model: an enterprise-wide foundation that makes agents, automation, and intelligent data routine. Because the alternative is exhausting: fighting tooth and nail to scale individual AI projects.

Unfortunately, exhaustion is the status quo.

Why? One reason is a misconception about who builds the AI Operating Model. Ask who owns AI, and every executive raises a hand: the CIO for the technology, the CAIO for the models, the CFO for the investment, the CHRO for the workforce.

In reality, it’s a joint effort across the C-suite. Still, someone must steward these efforts. Often that’s the COO, whose remit spans every function. But even the COO can’t make executive decisions across every business unit. Instead, they need to build consensus. And so a decidedly old-school skill – influence – is at the center of AI success today. Rolling up your sleeves and building relationships,…
items.t: Want to build an AI operating model? First, build consensus

items.title: Amazon and Google will own nearly 30% of Anthropic after today’s IPO, netting a roughly $260 billion paper windfall
items.summary:
Amazon and Google spent the last three years building AI models to compete with Anthropic. As of Thursday morning, they also own 28% of it.

When Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, Amazon will hold 14.6% of the Claude maker and Google 13.4%, according to Anthropic’s final prospectus . All of it is Class N stock, which has no vote. Anthropic’s seven co-founders keep control through a single share of a special class of stock, held by an LLC they organized. Google’s stake includes about $10 billion of a $26 billion private placement at the $83 IPO price, alongside Nvidia , Microsoft , AMD , Broadcom , Micron and TSMC . 

It’s evolving into a kind of frenemy relationship, or a coopetition, competition and cooperation bundled together. Amazon and Google rent Anthropic its chips, resell its models and keep a cut, and own a big piece of the equity, all while selling their own models against Claude.

Anthropic says in its filing that it has partnerships with Amazon, Google and Microsoft, which “simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors,” creating conflicts of interest it calls “difficult to fully anticipate or mitigate.” Lina Khan, who opened an FTC inquiry into these deals as the agency’s chair, told Axios this week the stakes create “the deep kind of conflicts” regulators worried about. 

Fortune ’s pricing story put Anthropic’s valuation at $1.5 trillion. At $83 a share, Amazon’s 1.94 billion shares are worth about $161 billion and Google’s 1.77 billion about $147 billion. Amazon has put about $18 billion…
items.t: Amazon and Google will own nearly 30% of Anthropic after today’s IPO, netting a roughly $260 billion paper windfall

items.title: Nvidia can run without Jensen Huang. Can the AI boom?
items.summary:
Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue: 

The downfall of AI’s $5.7 trillion man. 

Anthropic’s IPO is finally here. 

Government auditors got four top chatbots to help plan terror attacks. 

And a coalition says, “Anthropic is not a safe AI company.” 

In October, Jeremy Kahn and I sat down with Jensen Huang during his European tour. At the time, Huang looked less like a chip executive and more like the AI boom’s chief evangelist. His word moved markets, his keynotes filled arenas, and his company was at one point worth more than $5.7 trillion.

A month later, he was gone. For Fortune’s December/January magazine, we spoke with dozens of people to find out how Huang built his empire and what happens to it without him.

In a wide-ranging interview (before news of the scandal broke), Huang defended the company’s complex web of financing. Nvidia pours money into startups, AI labs, and cloud companies, which in part use that money to buy Nvidia chips. Critics called this process “circular financing,” saying it leaves much of the AI boom dangerously exposed to weak links that could topple the entire house of cards.

At that time, though, not even the company’s harshest critics thought the weak link could be the man at the center of it all: Huang.

The scandal took about two weeks to unfold. Reports emerged that U.S. officials believed Huang had been romantically involved with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore neocloud Megaspeed whom they suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang admitted to staff that he had been…
items.t: Nvidia can run without Jensen Huang. Can the AI boom?

items.title: Britain and the Pentagon told people to get ready in October. Now Costco is selling out of generators and billionaires have ‘apocalypse insurance’
items.summary:
Costco shoppers are “pantry-loading” again. As of Sunday night, 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators on Costco’s website were sold out, according to Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger. One of the sold-out models, a Kohler, runs about $7,000. 

The last time Costco members bought like this was March 2020, when then-CFO Richard Galanti told investors the buying was “off the charts” across the U.S. On March 12 of that year, U.S. toilet paper sales were up 734% from the same day a year earlier.

This time the buying picked up after a run of tech failures that has kept people out of their email, grounded flights and left bank customers unable to move money, and households are now spending to get ready for the next one. Bellinger told clients that consumer anxiety after the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stop for all U.S. airline flights and apocalyptic concerns flaring up on social media is behind the buying. He raised his Costco price target to $1,150 from $1,100 and said Walmart and Sam’s Club could see similar “pantry-loading lifts.”

What’s selling 

Costco CFO Gary Millerchip told Bloomberg that stronger sales of rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators and batteries came toward the end of October. Mizuho says Home Depot and Lowe’s could sell more generators, too.

Smaller sellers are seeing the same thing. Survival Frog, which sells emergency food, radios and other survival gear, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16 compared with prior weeks, CEO and founder Byron Walker told Axios . Most of the recent buyers were new customers, and…
items.t: Britain and the Pentagon told people to get ready in October. Now Costco is selling out of generators and billionaires have ‘apocalypse insurance’

items.title: ‘Anyone forecasting 2027 is forecasting data centers’: The Fed is about to hike into an AI boom it can’t cool, and Main Street gets the bill
items.summary:
The Federal Reserve is getting ready to raise interest rates again, after a hike in September. This time it’s pinning part of the blame on artificial intelligence.

Minutes from the Fed’s late-October meeting, released Wednesday, show “almost all” officials thought more rate hikes “would likely be appropriate.” The usual suspect was there: the “vast majority” said high energy prices were still feeding inflation. The new one was AI. “Many participants observed that demand for products associated with the AI buildout was continuing to strain supply and raise prices of technology-related consumer goods,” and several said the price pressure was spreading “beyond industries directly affected by data center construction.”

That meeting was held a week before the midterms. Measures restricting data centers passed in 44 places, from Ohio to Nevada, according to a Redbud Consulting count reported by U.S. News & World Report. . In Ohio, Sherrod Brown’s campaign ran an ad calling his opponent “the face of data centers.” Brown won. The governors-elect in Texas and Georgia have both talked about pausing new projects. In a Pew Research Center survey this summer, 60% of U.S. adults said they’d be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area.

Put those together and many Americans end up squeezed from both sides. Where data centers were on the ballot, voters rejected them.The Fed is now lining up to raise their borrowing costs, partly because of data centers. And those same data centers are still the biggest thing holding up the economy heading into next year.…
items.t: ‘Anyone forecasting 2027 is forecasting data centers’: The Fed is about to hike into an AI boom it can’t cool, and Main Street gets the bill

items.title: Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap, in mega IPO
items.summary:
Anthropic’s stock surged more than 30% in first minutes as a public company, a roaring debut that crowned the AI company—at least briefly—with a stunning, $2 trillion market cap.

Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Thursday, up 34% from the $83 IPO price. The stock pop began to moderate somewhat shortly afterward, with shares trading up 18%, at $97.76 per share.

At the $111.50 price, Anthropic’s market cap would be roughly $2 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies.

Shares of Anthropic, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” began trading a couple of hours after the stock market’s opening bell. The strong demand for Anthropic shares came as the broader market was under pressure, with the Nasdaq down 363 points and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 1038 points midday trading.

Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share , above its marketed range of $70 to $78, giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million.

There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion ($81.4 billion, if stock sold by insiders is included) would top the $75 billion raised by SpaceX.

There was tremendous demand for Anthropic’s shares,…
items.t: Anthropic set to begin trading any moment. Reports suggest stock could pop 20% or more in biggest IPO ever

With shares priced at $83 apiece, Anthropic employees now hold an estimated $232 billion in combined wealth—equivalent to roughly $44 million per employee.

The gains are particularly pronounced for employees who joined the San Francisco-based company early: at least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC , and several could join Anthropic’s seven cofounders in becoming billionaires .

If there’s a desire to cash out, non-founder employees can sell up to 10% of their stock on the first trading day, with another 35% becoming eligible for sale after the company’s 2026 earnings. This would add to the fortunes that have likely already soared in recent years thanks to highly competitive pay packages for AI talent .

The IPO will put Anthropic in the exclusive club of trillion-dollar companies, a group currently led by Apple , valued at $5.12 trillion. By valuation, Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion offering would rank as the second-largest in history, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO . But measured by capital raised, Anthropic comes out ahead: Its $81 billion surpasses the $75 billion SpaceX raised.

items.title: I’m the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally. Here’s what business leaders are wrestling with
items.summary:
For the past year, the conversation about enterprise AI and security has fixated on what region the models come from. It is a fair question. But as the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally, I often speak with the increasing number of business leaders adopting open models. Where their models come from is not the question that keeps them up at night.

What they worry about is more simple. They ask questions like, “Where does my data go when I use these models?”, “Who can see it?”, and “How long is it kept?”

These questions matter more than ever right now, and not just because of the latest string of hacks over the past month, including PHP2Shell which left millions of websites around the world vulnerable, but because of how AI is being used in businesses. Coding agents, security tools and internal assistants send enormous amounts of company information to a model: source code, internal documents, customer details, the context of a team’s daily work. Not only is this highly sensitive information for a business, but it’s also extremely valuable to anyone who wants to train a model of their own.

AI leaders are already bracing for what comes next. NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang made it a feature in his keynote at GTC Berlin, and Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer, recently warned that conditions would get worse before they improve, urging business leaders to take action. That action starts with knowing where company information goes when AI is used.

Most companies assume a vendor either protects their data or it…
items.t: I’m the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally. Here’s what business leaders are wrestling with

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours…

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.summary:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

  • Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

items.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
